image.alt: A Philodendron Burle Marx in a white pot, its glossy arrow-shaped green leaves fanning out on upright pale stems

light.label: Bright indirect light, or morning sun outdoors
light.note: Takes medium light indoors and morning sun outdoors

landscape_use.note: Frost-free zones, out of harsh afternoon sun

snap: A sprawling, clump-forming Philodendron with glossy arrow-shaped leaves on pale upright stems. It spreads sideways rather than climbing, forgives neglect better than most of the genus, and is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed.

deep_dive.title: Origin & Habit
deep_dive.body: Native to the Atlantic forest of eastern Brazil, and named for Roberto Burle Marx, the landscape architect who put Brazilian natives into gardens when the fashion was still European. It creeps rather than climbs — stems run along the surface and send up leaves as they go, so a plant widens before it heightens.

deep_dive.title: Key Care Rule
deep_dive.body: Water when the top inch of the mix has dried, in a loose aroid mix. The thick stems hold a reserve, so a missed week does no harm — soggy soil does. Of the two mistakes, this plant much prefers you forget it.

deep_dive.title: Special Feature
deep_dive.body: It makes more of itself. Each stem throws offsets at the base until one plant becomes a full clump, and a cut stem with a node roots in water in a few weeks. Split it every couple of years and you have gifts rather than a pot-bound plant.

deep_dive.title: Indoors Or Out
deep_dive.body: Indoors it fills a pot and holds its shape without a pole. In a frost-free garden it is a groundcover — planted in drifts under trees it knits into low, weed-smothering cover, which is exactly the use its namesake had in mind.
